entry.title: Sentry never ran on my Next.js server, and the dashboard looked fine
entry.summary:
I run Asermu, a novel-writing app built with Next.js and deployed as a Docker image on Railway. I added Sentry a while ago. The dashboard stayed quiet, and I took that as good news. It wasn't. Today I found that server-side Sentry had never started in production. Not once. I keep a flag-gated test route that reports a test error to Sentry on purpose. On the server runtime it returned: { "sent": true, "runtime": "nodejs", "eventId": "309ea78...", "flushOk": false }
captureException happily handed back an event id. But Sentry.flush() returned false, and nothing arrived in Sentry. The same test on the edge runtime returned flushOk: true, and its event showed up in Sentry. In 90 days, Sentry had received exactly one event: my own edge test. Zero real server errors is not the same as zero erro…

entry.title: The perceptron: the 1958 machine that learned from its mistakes
entry.summary: How one artificial neuron makes a decision, and how it fixes itself when it's wrong. In 1958, psychologist Frank Rosenblatt unveiled the perceptron at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory. The press got excited. The New York Times wrote that the Navy expected it to one day walk, talk, see, and write. It couldn't do any of that. But it introduced an idea that every modern neural network still uses: a machine that improves by fixing its own mistakes. Under the hood, a perceptron is a single artificial neuron. It does three things: It takes some inputs, like x₁ and x₂. It multiplies each input by a weight (w₁ and w₂) and adds them up. It compares the sum with a threshold, written θ (theta). If the sum clears the threshold, the perceptron outputs 1. Otherwise, it outputs 0. That's the whole dec…
